declared_proposition: For every prime q>5 define the integer Fermat quotients U=(2^(q-1)-1)/q and V=(3^(q-1)-1)/q, read modulo q^2. Then q^3 divides 32^(q-1)-27^(q-1) if and only if 5U-3V+q(10U^2-3V^2)=0 modulo q^2, while q^3 divides 2^(q-1)-3^(q-1) if and only if U-V=0 modulo q^2. Reduction modulo q recovers the TICKET-244 first-layer bad and comparison lines. These are exact second-order digit criteria, not an all-prime nonvanishing theorem.
mathematical_argument: Write 2^(q-1)=1+qU and 3^(q-1)=1+qV. Modulo q^3, the binomial theorem gives (1+qU)^5=1+5qU+10q^2U^2 and (1+qV)^3=1+3qV+3q^2V^2. Subtracting and dividing by q proves the first criterion. Direct subtraction of 1+qU and 1+qV proves the second. Only U,V modulo q^2 are needed. The computation checks both criteria against independent modular exponentiation modulo q^3.

reproducible_computation.no_go_scope: No first-layer bad prime occurs in the bounded scan, so the scan does not exercise the actual bad branch and cannot prove it empty. The formula decides depth three once q is supplied but gives no uniform control at arbitrary depth and no statement about general Collatz trajectories or nontrivial cycles.

finite_computation_boundary: The first layer is scanned for all 1,270,604 primes through 20,000,000; q^3 identities are replayed only through 50,000. Both use exact integer modular arithmetic, but neither finite boundary proves an all-prime statement.
logical_limit: No all-prime argument excludes the first bad line, and the second-order formula does not control arbitrary q-adic depths or general Collatz dynamics.

route_decision.discard: none newly; the finite absence of bad-line primes is not promoted to an all-prime theorem
route_decision.retain: exact higher q-adic digit formulas for the actual bases, while continuing adversarial search for a first bad-line prime

claim_boundary: No Collatz proof, divergent orbit, or nontrivial cycle; an exact q^3 criterion and bounded adversarial replay only.
